procedural_history.originating_court: Armed Forces Tribunal (AFT), Regional Bench, Mumbai
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 04.03.2015 of the Armed Forces Tribunal, Regional Bench, Mumbai in Original Application No. 55 of 2014, setting aside the finding of ‘guilty’ in respect of three charges (8th, 9th and 10th)
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Both the officer and the Union of India filed appeals before the Supreme Court after the AFT declined their request for leave to appeal, stating that no question of law of public importance was involved. The Supreme Court clubbed the appeals together, stayed the operation of the AFT order while issuing notice in the appeal filed by the respondent (officer), admitted both appeals on July 01, 2016, directed expedited hearing, and continued the interim order. The Supreme Court then heard both sides at length and dismissed both appeals.

directions: As a consequence, both the appeals are dismissed.

The respondent herein shall be reinstated in service within 2 weeks from the date of passing of this order and he shall not be entitled to any salary for the intervening period, i.e., from the date of dismissal till the date of reinstatement.
There shall be no orders as to costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the prosecution has been able to give satisfactory proof to prove that when the offending calls in question were made, the Cell Phone with Mobile No. 9564784782 was with the respondent.

facts: The respondent was accused of making explicit sexual calls to three Navy officers' wives from Vodafone Mobile No. 9564784782.
The respondent admitted to purchasing the SIM card with this number but claimed it was for his wife and that it had been lost before the calls were made.
The respondent traveled by flight from Mumbai to Kochi on June 29, 2011.
Call Data Records (CDRs) were presented as evidence by the prosecution.
application: The Court rejected the respondent's explanation that the SIM card was lost or used by his wife, finding it not credible.

The Court relied on CDR evidence that showed calls were made from the mobile number even after the date the respondent's wife reported it lost. For instance, calls were made to another officer's number on dates when the SIM was supposedly missing.

The most crucial piece of evidence was the phone's location tracking the respondent's travel. On June 29, 2011, a call was made from the phone in the Mumbai area shortly before the respondent's flight departed. Another call was made from the same phone from the Kerala area shortly after his flight landed in Kochi.
The Court found that this travel evidence proved "beyond any reasonable doubt" that the cell phone was with the respondent and not lost or with anyone else.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the prosecution successfully proved that the cell phone with Mobile No. 9564784782 was in the respondent's possession when the offending calls were made. This was established primarily through call records that contradicted the respondent's claim of a lost SIM and, most significantly, by evidence showing the phone's location matched the respondent's own travel itinerary from Mumbai to Kochi.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the prosecution has been able to give satisfactory proof to prove that when the offending calls in question were made, the Cell Phone with Mobile No. 9564784782 was with the respondent.
appellant_arguments: The prosecution (appellant) argued that they had provided satisfactory proof that the offending calls from Mobile No. 9564784782 were made by the respondent and that the cell phone was with him at the time.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the prosecution had failed to provide satisfactory proof that he was in possession of the cell phone with Mobile No. 9564784782 when the calls in question were made.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: While the court agreed with the prosecution that it had provided satisfactory proof that the cell phone was with the respondent when the offending calls were made, it ultimately dismissed the Union of India's appeal regarding the quantum of sentence. The court found that the Armed Forces Tribunal's decision to substitute the punishment of dismissal with forfeiture of seniority was a reasonable exercise of discretion, especially since the respondent had also been deprived of his salary for over five years, concluding that this combined effect would "meet the ends of justice."
legal_tests_applied: In reviewing the Tribunal's finding of guilt, the court assessed whether the conclusion was "utterly perverse which no reasonable person could have arrived at."
In reviewing the Tribunal's decision on the quantum of sentence, the court assessed whether the "discretion exercised by the Tribunal does not need any interference."
why_appellant_lost: The court was not inclined to interfere with the Tribunal's order on the sentence because the combined effect of the punishment was significant: the respondent's seniority was forfeited by 24 months, and he was also deprived of his salary for more than five years.

The court concluded that the sentence imposed by the Tribunal, when viewed in its entirety including the loss of pay, was sufficient to meet the ends of justice, and therefore the Tribunal's exercise of discretion did not warrant interference.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's appeal against the finding of guilt was dismissed because the court found no infirmity in the Tribunal's conclusion, stating that it was not "utterly perverse."

The respondent succeeded in having the Union of India's appeal dismissed because the Supreme Court agreed with the Tribunal that the punishment of dismissal was disproportionate, and that the lesser sentence of forfeiture of seniority, combined with the loss of over five years' salary, was an adequate punishment that met the ends of justice.
policy_considerations: The court considered the proportionality of the sentence, weighing the proven charges against the severity of the punishment, and determined that the modified sentence would "meet the ends of justice."

The court took into account the practical and financial consequences of the prolonged litigation, noting that the respondent being "deprived of his salary for more than five years" was a significant factor in determining that the overall punishment was sufficient.
